note: Phases follow the published standards named in each discipline, down to the test ID where the standard has one. Commands use the tools in this catalogue where they fit; where a tool is not built yet the command is still correct but has no page to link to.

frameworks.name: PTES
frameworks.summary: Seven phases covering a whole engagement, from the pre-engagement conversation to the report. The most widely used general structure, and the one most other methodologies slot into.

frameworks.name: OSSTMM 3
frameworks.full: Open Source Security Testing Methodology Manual
frameworks.summary: ISECOM's standard, and the only one here that is about measurement rather than findings. A RAV (Risk Assessment Value) scores attack surface against the controls protecting it, so two testers assessing the same target should land on comparable numbers. Reports go out in the STAR format. The four phases run over five channels, not just networks.

frameworks.name: OWASP WSTG
frameworks.summary: The reference for web testing. Every test has an identifier — WSTG-INFO-02, WSTG-ATHN-03 — which is what you cite in a report so a reader can look up exactly what you did.

frameworks.name: OWASP MASTG
frameworks.summary: The mobile counterpart, paired with MASVS which sets the requirement levels. Split by platform because the tooling barely overlaps.

frameworks.name: NIST SP 800-115
frameworks.full: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
frameworks.summary: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment. Broader than a pentest standard: a pentest is one technique among several. Execution runs four technique categories in order of impact, passive to active, and not every engagement needs to reach the last one. Guidance, not regulation — it mandates no testing frequency, unlike PCI DSS.

frameworks.name: CREST
frameworks.full: Council of Registered Ethical Security Testers
frameworks.summary: Less a test methodology than a standard for how the engagement is run: scoping, consent, tester competence, evidence handling, reporting quality. What a client buys when they buy a CREST-accredited test.

frameworks.name: PCI DSS 4.0
frameworks.summary: Compliance-driven, so the rules are specific: at least annually and after any significant change, internal and external, network and application layer, plus explicit segmentation testing at least every six months.

frameworks.name: ISSAF
frameworks.summary: OISSG, v0.2.1, last published around 2006 and no longer maintained — there is no official download left. Worth knowing for the nine-step assessment model inside its middle phase, which is still the clearest map of how an attacker actually progresses: steps 1-3 recon, 4-7 active compromise, 8-9 persistence and stealth. Study the logic, not its tool advice.

frameworks.name: MITRE ATT&CK
frameworks.full: Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge
frameworks.summary: Not a test methodology — a shared vocabulary for what attackers do. You map findings to it so a blue team can say which techniques they would have caught.

frameworks.name: CSA CCM
frameworks.summary: Cloud Security Alliance. A governance and compliance control set, not a testing methodology: 17 domains mapped across ISO 27001, NIST and PCI DSS. Reach for it when a client wants to know whether their cloud configuration meets a standard, rather than whether you can break into it.

frameworks.name: CBEST
frameworks.summary: Bank of England, with the UK financial sector. Starts with a bespoke threat intelligence phase that names the threat actors relevant to that specific institution, and the test then simulates those scenarios. Regulator-backed, and nothing general-purpose substitutes for it when a UK bank is in scope.

frameworks.name: WASC TC
frameworks.summary: Web Application Security Consortium. A taxonomy for naming web attack classes that mattered in the mid-2000s and has since been superseded by the OWASP Top Ten and WSTG. You will meet it in old reports and in compliance documents that were never rewritten.

disciplines.name: Web application
disciplines.summary: OWASP WSTG v4.2, its twelve test categories in order. Each phase names the WSTG IDs it covers so a finding maps straight to a report reference.

phases.name: Information gathering
phases.goal: Know everything that exists before testing any of it. Most missed findings are on surfaces nobody enumerated.

steps.why: What the target already leaks publicly: indexed admin pages, robots.txt, sitemap, security.txt.

cmds.text: site:target.example.com -www   (Google dork for subdomains and stray pages)

steps.why: Version information narrows everything after it, and is sometimes the finding itself.
Admin panels, backups, old versions and .git are found here or not at all.
A second host in scope is a second attack surface. Virtual hosts hide behind the same IP.

phases.name: Configuration and deployment
phases.goal: The server and platform around the application: methods, headers, exposed files, cloud buckets.

steps.why: TRACE, PUT and PATCH left on, missing HSTS, missing or weak CSP. Each is a quick, citable finding.
An editor backup of a config file hands over database credentials in one request.
Management panels and world-readable buckets. Subdomain takeover lives here too.

cmds.text: aws s3 ls s3://target-assets --no-sign-request   (open bucket check)

steps.why: Protocol versions, cipher suites, certificate validity. Overlaps with the cryptography phase.

phases.name: Identity and authentication
phases.goal: Who the application thinks you are and how it decides. Registration, enumeration, login, lockout, reset, MFA.

steps.why: A login or reset form that answers differently for a real account turns a password spray into a targeted one.

cmds.text: compare the response and timing for a known-good versus a random username

steps.why: Default admin accounts and credentials sent in the clear. Check the login posts over TLS first.
steps.warn: Credential attacks against an account you do not own need explicit written scope. Lockout policy (WSTG-ATHN-03) can lock out real users.

steps.why: Reset tokens that do not expire, host-header poisoning of the reset link, MFA that can be skipped.

cmds.text: request a reset twice; check whether the first token still works

phases.name: Authorization
phases.goal: Whether the application enforces what each identity is allowed to do. IDOR, traversal, privilege escalation, OAuth.

steps.why: A path parameter that reaches outside the web root reads /etc/passwd or application source.
Incrementing an id in a URL or body returns another user's record. The highest-frequency real-world web bug.

cmds.text: log in as two low-privilege users; swap ids between their sessions

steps.why: A low-privilege session reaching an admin endpoint, or a role field the client controls.

cmds.text: repeat every privileged request with a lower-privileged session and with no session

phases.name: Session management
phases.goal: How the application issues, protects and ends sessions. Cookie flags, fixation, CSRF, JWT, timeout.

steps.why: Missing HttpOnly, Secure or SameSite turns an XSS into full account theft.
A state-changing request with no unpredictable token, or a session id that survives login.

cmds.text: submit a state-changing form with the CSRF token removed and with another user's token

steps.why: alg:none accepted, a weak HMAC secret, or the signature never checked.

cmds.text: decode the three base64 segments; try alg:none and re-sign

phases.name: Input validation and injection
phases.goal: The largest category. Every place user input reaches an interpreter: SQL, OS, LDAP, XML, template, XSS.

steps.why: You cannot test an injection point you have not found. Enumerate GET, POST and JSON parameters.
From a single quote that errors to full extraction. Confirm by hand, then let the tool enumerate.
steps.warn: --dump and --os-shell change or read data. Stay within scope and keep --threads modest on production.

steps.why: Reflected, stored and DOM-based. The payload lists under the XSS tab feed this step.

cmds.text: inject a unique marker; grep the response and any stored view for it unescaped

steps.why: Where input reaches a shell or eval. A sleep that delays the response confirms blind execution.

cmds.text: try ; sleep 5 and | sleep 5 and $(sleep 5); a 5-second delay confirms it

phases.name: Error handling and cryptography
phases.goal: What the application leaks when it breaks, and whether its transport and stored crypto hold up.

steps.why: A stack trace names the framework, file paths and sometimes credentials.
Old TLS, weak ciphers, sensitive data over plain HTTP, home-made crypto.

phases.name: Business logic
phases.goal: Flaws the scanner cannot see because every request is individually valid. The sequence is the bug.

steps.why: Skipping a step, replaying a one-time action, a negative quantity that credits the account.

cmds.text: complete a checkout, then replay the final request; change quantity to -1
reach step 3 of a wizard directly, without completing step 1 and 2

steps.why: An upload that accepts a server-executable file is a web shell. The Web shells tab has the payloads.

cmds.text: try double extensions (shell.php.jpg), null bytes, and content-type spoofing

steps.warn: Uploading a shell to a system you do not own is intrusion. Scope it, and remove it afterwards.

phases.name: Client-side
phases.goal: Code that runs in the browser: DOM XSS, CORS, clickjacking, postMessage, storage, tabnabbing.

steps.why: A permissive Access-Control-Allow-Origin, or no X-Frame-Options, exposes data and enables clickjacking.
Data flowing from location or postMessage into innerHTML or eval, and secrets in localStorage.

cmds.text: grep the JavaScript for document.write, innerHTML, eval, location.hash
read localStorage and sessionStorage in the browser console after login

phases.name: API testing
phases.goal: REST and GraphQL endpoints. Object-level and function-level authorization are where APIs break.

steps.why: Find the spec, the versions and the undocumented routes.
The API equivalent of IDOR, and the top item on the OWASP API Top 10.

cmds.text: request another user's object id with your own token

steps.why: Introspection left on hands over the entire schema.

phases.name: Reporting
phases.goal: The deliverable. Every finding with a WSTG id, evidence, impact and a fix a developer can act on.

steps.why: Executive summary for the business, technical detail for the fixers, each finding mapped to its WSTG id.

cmds.text: per finding: WSTG id, affected URL/parameter, request and response evidence, impact, remediation
rank by exploitability and impact, not by scanner severity

disciplines.name: Network and infrastructure
disciplines.summary: PTES phases over an internal or external network, with NIST SP 800-115's passive-to-active progression. Scope and rules of engagement first, every time.

phases.name: Scoping and rules of engagement
phases.goal: Agree what is in scope, the testing window and the emergency contact before a single packet. Unclear scope is the top source of disputes.

steps.why: A written target list and a signed authorization. The difference between a pentest and an intrusion.

cmds.text: record the in-scope ranges, the excluded hosts, the window, and who to call if something breaks
keep the authorization letter to hand for the whole engagement

phases.name: Host discovery
phases.goal: What is alive. A fast sweep first, so the slow scans only run against hosts that answer.

steps.why: A ping and ARP sweep is faster and quieter than port-scanning dead space.
On an internal engagement, listening finds hosts a scan would miss and makes no noise.

cmds.text: responder -A -I eth0   (analyse mode: watch broadcasts, send nothing)

phases.name: Port and service enumeration
phases.goal: What is listening, and what it is. Service and version detection turns an open port into a target.

steps.why: All 65535 ports, because the finding is often on a high port nobody scans.
DNS, SNMP, TFTP, IKE and NetBIOS live on UDP and are routinely skipped.
Each open service has its own enumeration. SMB, web and databases are the highest-value.

phases.name: Vulnerability analysis
phases.goal: Turn the service list into a list of things worth trying. Automated scan, then manual confirmation to kill false positives.

steps.why: Version-matched CVEs and misconfigurations. Everything here is a hypothesis until confirmed.
A scanner says 'possible'. You say 'confirmed', with the exact request that proves it.

cmds.text: reproduce each candidate finding manually before it goes near the report
a crashed service is an availability finding; note it, do not repeat it on production

phases.name: Exploitation
phases.goal: Prove the finding. Take only what the scope allows, and demonstrate impact rather than collecting shells.

steps.why: The confirmed vulnerability, exploited to the minimum needed to show it is real.

cmds.text: catch the callback with the Shells tab listener and payload

steps.warn: Exploitation is the point of no return for scope. Only what is authorized, only on the agreed hosts.

steps.why: Spraying one password across many accounts avoids lockout better than many passwords on one.
steps.warn: Lockout policy can disrupt real users. Agree the threshold in scoping and stay under it.

phases.name: Post-exploitation
phases.goal: Determine real-world impact. Pivot, escalate, and translate technical access into business risk.

steps.why: Who am I, what can I reach, what is stored here. The privesc checklists under Tools feed this.

cmds.text: upgrade the shell to a TTY first — see the Shells tab, Upgrade a shell

steps.why: From one host to the next, and from user to administrator. Stop at the agreed depth.

cmds.text: enumerate reachable internal hosts from the foothold
harvest credentials; test them across the estate with netexec

phases.name: Reporting
phases.goal: The deliverable a third party can re-run. Executive summary plus per-finding technical detail.

steps.why: Business impact in plain language for leadership; exact reproduction for the people who fix it.

cmds.text: per finding: host, port, evidence, impact, remediation, and a severity you can defend
include the scope, the window, and anything you could not reach and why

disciplines.name: Mobile
disciplines.summary: OWASP MASTG, structured by the eight MASVS v2 control groups. Android and iOS; the tests differ by platform but the controls are the same.

phases.name: Gather the artefacts
phases.goal: Get the package and know what is inside it before testing anything.

steps.why: The APK or IPA is the starting point. Decompile it to read what it ships with.

cmds.text: adb shell pm path <package>; adb pull <path>   (Android)
apktool d app.apk   ·   jadx -d out app.apk

steps.why: Exported components, debug flags, permissions and backup settings are all declared here.

phases.name: Storage and cryptography
phases.goal: What the application keeps on the device, and how badly it keeps it.

steps.why: Credentials and tokens in shared preferences, SQLite, plists or logs. The most common mobile finding.

cmds.text: strings app databases and shared_prefs for tokens, keys and passwords
check /sdcard and external storage, which any app can read

steps.why: Hard-coded keys, ECB mode, or secrets not held in the Keystore/Keychain.

cmds.text: grep the decompiled source for SecretKeySpec, IvParameterSpec, 'AES/ECB'
confirm keys come from the Android Keystore or iOS Keychain, not a constant

phases.name: Authentication and network
phases.goal: How the app authenticates, and whether anyone on the path can read or alter its traffic.

steps.why: TLS, and whether the app pins its certificate. No pinning means a proxy sees everything.

cmds.text: route the device through mitmproxy; a connection that still works has no pinning

steps.why: Tokens that never expire, biometric checks done only in the UI, auth decided on the client.

cmds.text: capture the login API call; replay it after logout to test token lifetime
check whether a biometric prompt gates a client flag or a server-side secret

phases.name: Platform and code
phases.goal: How the app uses the platform, and the quality of what shipped.

steps.why: Exported activities, services and content providers that other apps can reach.

cmds.text: adb shell am start -n <package>/<exported.activity>   (reach an exported screen)
drozer: run app.provider.finduri <package> to find queryable providers

steps.why: Debuggable builds, verbose logging, outdated libraries with known CVEs.

cmds.text: adb logcat | grep <package>   (secrets printed to the log)
list bundled libraries and versions; check each against known CVEs

phases.name: Resilience and privacy
phases.goal: Anti-tampering for apps that need it, and what personal data the app collects and sends.

steps.why: Root/jailbreak detection, debugger detection, obfuscation. Relevant where the threat model needs it.

cmds.text: run on a rooted device; see whether the app refuses to start
frida-trace the detection routines to test whether they can be bypassed

steps.why: What identifiers and personal data leave the device, and to whom.

cmds.text: capture all outbound traffic; list every third-party host and what is sent to it

phases.name: Reporting
phases.goal: Findings mapped to MASVS controls, with platform noted, evidence, and a fix.

steps.why: Each finding against its MASVS control, Android or iOS, with the exact artefact as evidence.

cmds.text: per finding: MASVS control, platform, file or endpoint, evidence, impact, remediation

disciplines.name: Cloud and containers
disciplines.summary: Cloud posture and container security. A controls assessment against CSA CCM, plus the hands-on checks for exposed storage, IAM and container escape.

phases.name: Enumerate the footprint
phases.ref: CSA CCM — Governance · PTES — Intelligence gathering
phases.goal: What the organisation exposes in the cloud before you touch any of it.

steps.what: Find the provider and the public surface
steps.why: DNS, certificate transparency and reverse lookups reveal the cloud estate.

cmds.text: dig +short CNAME <host>   (points at cloudfront, azureedge, etc.)
cloud_enum -k <org>   ·   check crt.sh for the org's certificates

steps.why: World-readable buckets and blobs are the single most common cloud finding.

phases.name: Identity and access
phases.goal: Who can do what. Over-permissive roles and exposed keys are where cloud engagements turn.

steps.why: A leaked access key or an over-broad role is full compromise. Enumerate what the identity can do.

cmds.text: aws sts get-caller-identity   (whose key is this)

steps.warn: Only with keys you were given for the engagement. Enumerating IAM you were not scoped for is intrusion.

phases.name: Container and orchestration
phases.goal: The Docker and Kubernetes layer. Misconfigured daemons and permissive pods lead to the host.

steps.why: An exposed Docker API or a privileged container is a path to the node.
An open kubelet or dashboard, and over-permissive service accounts.

cmds.text: kubectl auth can-i --list   (what this token can do)

phases.name: Reporting
phases.ref: CSA CCM — Audit and assurance · PTES — Reporting
phases.goal: Findings mapped to CCM domains, with the control that was missing and the fix.

steps.why: Each finding against its CCM domain, with evidence and the specific configuration to change.

cmds.text: per finding: CCM domain, resource, misconfiguration, impact, remediation

disciplines.name: Wireless
disciplines.summary: 802.11 wireless testing: discover the networks, capture the handshake, test the encryption, and check client and enterprise exposure. OSSTMM's wireless channel.

phases.name: Prepare the interface
phases.goal: Monitor mode is the prerequisite for everything else. Nothing works without it.

steps.why: Put the adapter into monitor mode and confirm no process will interfere.

phases.name: Discover networks and clients
phases.ref: OSSTMM — Wireless channel · PTES — Intelligence gathering
phases.goal: Every access point and associated client in range, with its channel, encryption and signal.

steps.why: The access points, their encryption, and which clients are talking to them.

phases.name: Capture and test encryption
phases.goal: The WPA handshake, then an offline test of the passphrase. Never online against the AP.

steps.why: Wait for a client to connect, or deauthenticate one to force a reconnect.

cmds.text: tshark -r capture.cap -Y 'eapol'   (confirm the 4-way handshake is captured)

steps.warn: Deauthentication knocks real users offline. Only in scope, and only the target BSSID.

steps.why: A dictionary test of the captured handshake. Offline, so the AP never sees it.

phases.name: Enterprise and client attacks
phases.goal: WPA-Enterprise and the clients themselves: evil twin, PMKID, and credential capture.

steps.why: PMKID needs no client. Enterprise networks expose credentials to a rogue RADIUS.
steps.warn: An evil twin captures real users' credentials. This needs explicit, specific authorization.

phases.name: Reporting
phases.goal: Each network, its encryption, what was recoverable, and the remediation.

steps.why: Per network: BSSID, encryption, whether the passphrase or credentials were recovered, and the fix.

cmds.text: per finding: SSID/BSSID, encryption type, what was recovered, impact, remediation

disciplines.name: PCI DSS
disciplines.summary: PCI DSS v4.0 Requirement 11.4. A regulated scope: the methodology is documented, segmentation is proven, and both the external perimeter and internal network are tested.

phases.name: Define and document the methodology
phases.goal: 11.4.1 requires a defined, documented penetration-testing methodology before testing. This is a compliance gate, not a formality.

steps.why: Everything that stores, processes or transmits card data, plus every system connected to it.

cmds.text: map the CDE: card data stores, processing systems, and connected-to systems
document the methodology, coverage, and the retention of results 11.4.1 requires

phases.name: Internal penetration test
phases.goal: 11.4.2: an internal test, at least annually and after significant change, at network and application layer.

steps.why: The perspective of an attacker already on the internal network.

cmds.text: test the in-scope applications to the depth the web discipline covers

phases.name: External penetration test
phases.goal: 11.4.3: an external test of the perimeter, at least annually and after significant change.

steps.why: The attacker's view of the perimeter: exposed services, the web application, and remote access.

cmds.text: test any exposed web application and VPN/remote-access endpoint

phases.name: Correct and retest
phases.goal: 11.4.4: exploitable vulnerabilities and weaknesses found are corrected, and testing is repeated to verify the fix.

steps.why: A finding is not closed until a re-test proves it. This is required, not optional.

cmds.text: re-run the exact test that found each issue, after the fix
record the before, the change, and the after for each corrected finding

phases.name: Segmentation testing
phases.goal: 11.4.5: prove the CDE is isolated from out-of-scope networks, at least every twelve months — or every six (11.4.6) if you are a service provider.

steps.why: From an out-of-scope network, confirm nothing in the CDE is reachable. A single open path fails it.

cmds.text: nmap -sS -Pn -p- 10.20.0.0/24 -oA pci/segmentation   (run from outside the CDE)
test every out-of-scope segment that should have no route into the CDE

phases.name: Reporting
phases.goal: A report that satisfies the assessor: methodology, scope, findings, remediation and the segmentation result.

steps.why: Mapped to the 11.4 sub-requirements, with the evidence an assessor needs to sign it off.

cmds.text: per finding: 11.4 reference, system, evidence, correction, and re-test result
state the segmentation test result and the methodology used explicitly

choosing.intro: Nobody picks one framework and uses it for everything. A real engagement has a primary methodology that structures the work, plus whatever the client's industry, platform or regulator forces on top. Four things decide it.

criteria.name: What you are testing
criteria.detail: The first and bluntest filter. A web app points at OWASP WSTG. A mobile app points at MASTG. A whole corporate network points at PTES or OSSTMM. A scope that includes people and buildings, not just hosts, points at OSSTMM and its five channels.

criteria.name: What the regulator says
criteria.detail: This overrides what you would have preferred. Cardholder data means PCI DSS Requirement 11.4, whatever else you run. A UK bank under Bank of England oversight means CBEST. A US federal system means NIST SP 800-115 carries the weight.

criteria.name: Whether the numbers have to be comparable
criteria.detail: If the client wants to compare this year to last year, or compare two different firms, you need a measurement layer. That is what OSSTMM's RAVs are for, and no other framework here gives you it.

criteria.name: What your team can actually run
criteria.detail: The constraint people skip. A full OSSTMM needs real fluency in its metrics. CBEST needs a threat intelligence capability. For a small team on a standard network job, PTES gives the structure without the overhead.

scenarios.q: A regional hospital wants its patient portal and the internal network behind it tested. HIPAA applies. Payments are outsourced. The board wants a summary it can read.
scenarios.why: It covers the whole engagement end to end, and its reporting phase explicitly produces both an executive summary and a technical report, which is exactly what a board plus an IT team needs. Use OWASP WSTG for the portal test cases, and tag the findings with MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs so the security team can go and build detections.

scenarios.q: A multinational bank headquartered in London needs a test that satisfies its UK regulator, starting from a threat intelligence assessment of that institution.
scenarios.why: It is built for UK financial institutions, it mandates the bespoke threat intelligence phase they are describing, and it is the one the Bank of England recognises. No general-purpose framework satisfies that on its own.

scenarios.q: A SaaS startup wants two different security firms to test its web platform over two years and compare the results directly to see whether it improved.
scenarios.a: OSSTMM for the measurement, WSTG for the tests.
scenarios.why: 'Did we improve?' is a measurement question, and RAVs are the only thing here that makes two separate firms' results comparable. WSTG supplies the web test cases underneath that measurement layer.

scenarios.q: A fintech wants its Android and iOS banking apps tested. Both handle card transactions.
scenarios.why: MASTG gives you the mobile test cases for both platforms. PCI DSS applies the moment cardholder data is in play, and it is not optional. You satisfy the testing methodology and the regulatory mandate at the same time.

scenarios.q: A US federal agency wants its internal network assessed, aligned to federal guidance, covering document review as well as active testing.
scenarios.why: It is the federally recognised one, and it is deliberately broader than a pentest standard: its execution phase runs from reviewing policies and firewall rules through to exploitation, so document review and active testing live in the same methodology.

scenarios.q: An e-commerce company has a web storefront, a mobile shopping app, and a payment system.
scenarios.why: Three components, three references. WSTG for the storefront, MASTG for the app, and PCI DSS over the top because the payment system puts cardholder data in scope. PTES underneath keeps the engagement itself structured.
